claim: Interacting molecules create regulatory architectures that can persist despite turnover of molecules.
source: Interacting molecules create regulatory architectures that can persist despite turnover of molecules.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that frames the entire study.

claim: Information contained in regulatory architectures grows rapidly with the number of interacting molecules.
source: Information contained in regulatory architectures grows rapidly with the number of interacting molecules and its transmission requires positive feedback loops.
evidence: This claim is supported by calculations shown in Table 1 and discussed in the Results section.

claim: Transmission of information in regulatory architectures requires positive feedback loops.
source: Information contained in regulatory architectures grows rapidly with the number of interacting molecules and its transmission requires positive feedback loops.
evidence: This is derived from theoretical analysis of heritable regulatory architectures presented in the manuscript.

claim: Regulatory architectures can recover after many epigenetic perturbations.
source: While these architectures can recover after many epigenetic perturbations, some resulting changes can become permanently heritable.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 2 and related supplementary figures.

claim: Some epigenetic changes resulting from perturbations can become permanently heritable.
source: While these architectures can recover after many epigenetic perturbations, some resulting changes can become permanently heritable.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations and theoretical analysis in the Results section.

claim: Architectures that are otherwise unstable can become heritable through periodic interactions with external regulators.
source: Architectures that are otherwise unstable can become heritable through periodic interactions with external regulators, which suggests that mortal somatic lineages with cells that reproducibly interact with the immortal germ lineage could make a wider variety of architectures heritable.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 4 and related analysis.

claim: Mortal somatic lineages with cells that reproducibly interact with the immortal germ lineage could make a wider variety of architectures heritable.
source: Architectures that are otherwise unstable can become heritable through periodic interactions with external regulators, which suggests that mortal somatic lineages with cells that reproducibly interact with the immortal germ lineage could make a wider variety of architectures heritable.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the simulation results about periodic rescue.

claim: Differential inhibition of positive feedback loops that transmit regulatory architectures across generations can explain gene-specific differences in heritable RNA silencing observed in C. elegans.
source: Differential inhibition of the positive feedback loops that transmit regulatory architectures across generations can explain the gene-specific differences in heritable RNA silencing observed in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of experimental data from Devanapally et al., 2021 and theoretical modeling shown in Figure 6.

claim: The localization and activity of many kinds of molecules are recreated in successive generations during comparable stages.
source: For example, the localization and activity of many kinds of molecules are recreated in successive generations during comparable stages (Jose, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Recurring patterns can change throughout development such that following the levels and/or localizations of each kind of molecule over time traces waveforms that return in phase with the similarity of form and function across generations.
source: These recurring patterns can change throughout development such that following the levels and/or localizations of each kind of molecule over time traces waveforms that return in phase with the similarity of form and function across generations (Jose, 2020c).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The minimal heritable regulatory architecture is formed by two molecules that mutually promote each other's production, resulting in a positive feedback loop.
source: Therefore, the minimal heritable regulatory architecture (HRA) is that formed by two molecules that mutually promote each other's production (Figure 1, 'A'), resulting in a positive feedback loop.
evidence: This is derived from theoretical considerations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Not all positive feedback loops form heritable regulatory architectures.
source: However, not all positive feedback loops form HRAs.
evidence: This is explained with an example of mutual repression that leads to transient amplification.

claim: Positive feedback loops that promote transient amplification of changes are not compatible with perpetual inheritance because both molecules will be eventually lost by dilution or turnover.
source: For example, positive feedback loops that promote the transient amplification of changes such as that formed by two molecules that mutually repress each other's production (Mitrophanov and Groisman, 2008) are not compatible with perpetual inheritance because both molecules will be eventually lost by dilution or turnover.
evidence: This is explained through theoretical reasoning and supported by a citation.

claim: Two entities form one heritable regulatory architecture.
source: two entities form one HRA
evidence: This is stated as a result of computational enumeration shown in Table 1.

claim: Three entities form 25 heritable regulatory architectures.
source: three form 25
evidence: This is stated as a result of computational enumeration shown in Table 1.

claim: Four entities form 5604 heritable regulatory architectures.
source: and four form 5604
evidence: This is stated as a result of computational enumeration shown in Table 1.

claim: With four interactors, the maximal information that can be transmitted using HRAs (approximately 12.45 bits) surpasses that transmitted by a four base-pair long genome (8 bits).
source: Thus, with four interactors, the maximal information that can be transmitted using HRAs (log2[5604] ≈12.45 bits) surpasses that transmitted by a four base-pair long genome (log2[4].4 = 8 bits).
evidence: This is calculated from the enumeration results shown in Table 1.

claim: The combinatorial growth in the numbers of HRAs with the number of interactors can provide vastly more capacity for storing information in larger HRAs compared to that afforded by the proportional growth in longer genomes.
source: The combinatorial growth in the numbers of HRAs with the number of interactors can thus provide vastly more capacity for storing information in larger HRAs compared to that afforded by the proportional growth in longer genomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of information storage capacities.

claim: Genetic and epigenetic perturbations can generate different heritable changes.
source: Genetic and epigenetic perturbations can generate different heritable changes
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: The most widely used perturbation that is easy to accomplish using current experimental techniques is reducing the concentration of an entity/sensor.
source: Of these, the most widely used perturbation that is easy to accomplish using current experimental techniques is reducing the concentration of an entity/sensor (e.g. using a loss-of-function mutation, knockdown of an mRNA, degradation of a protein, etc.).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of common experimental practices.

claim: Genome editing for removal and RNA interference for reduction of an entity/sensor are common during the experimental analysis of living systems.
source: Indeed, the use of genome editing (Anzalone et al., 2020) for removal and RNA interference (RNAi) (Fire et al., 1998) for reduction of an entity/sensor are common during the experimental analysis of living systems.
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant methodological papers.

claim: Genetic change can result in unrestrained growth or eventual decay of the remaining entities depending on the residual architecture.
source: Thus, genetic change can result in unrestrained growth or eventual decay of the remaining entities depending on the residual architecture (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: Epigenetic change can result in unrestrained growth, eventual decay, or recovery at a new steady state level of the remaining entities depending on the residual architecture and the nature of the perturbation.
source: Thus, epigenetic change can result in unrestrained growth, eventual decay, or recovery at a new steady state level of the remaining entities depending on the residual architecture and the nature of the perturbation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: HRAs that are nearly indistinguishable by genetic perturbation can be distinguished using epigenetic perturbations.
source: HRAs that are nearly indistinguishable by genetic perturbation can be distinguished using epigenetic perturbations, underscoring the complementary nature of genetic and epigenetic perturbations.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results comparing genetic and epigenetic perturbations.

claim: The 26 HRAs can be mutated to generate 61 different changes.
source: With these considerations, enumeration of the changed HRAs that can result from a perturbation revealed that the 26 HRAs can be mutated to generate 61 different changes (24 through loss of interaction alone, 21 through change in polarity of interaction alone, and 16 through either change in regulation or though loss of an entity, with density of the change matrix ≈0.19 [61/325]).
evidence: This is stated as a result of enumeration shown in Figure 3.

claim: Unlike changes in DNA sequence, not all changes are immediately accessible among HRAs (change matrix of 1 vs 0.19, respectively).
source: Thus, unlike changes in DNA sequence, not all changes are immediately accessible among HRAs (change matrix of 1 vs 0.19, respectively).
evidence: This is calculated from the enumeration of possible changes.

claim: The heritable information transmitted using regulatory architectures is vast because even two or three interactors can form 26 heritable architectures that are collectively capable of 61 changes through single perturbations.
source: Nevertheless, the heritable information transmitted using regulatory architectures is vast because even two or three interactors can form 26 heritable architectures that are collectively capable of 61 changes through single perturbations.
evidence: This is inferred from the enumeration results.

claim: Single mutations can result in the gain of new interactions that combine multiple HRAs into larger regulatory architectures with more interactors.
source: This capacity is an underestimate because, single mutations can also result in the gain of new interactions that combine multiple HRAs into larger regulatory architectures with more interactors.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about additional possibilities not fully explored.

claim: HRAs that rely on all components for their production cannot change into any other HRAs from steady state without the addition of more positive regulation.
source: Furthermore, HRAs that rely on all components for their production ('C', 'F', 'H', 'K', and 'T') cannot change into any other HRAs from steady state without the addition of more positive regulation because any permanent loss in regulation without compensatory changes in turnover will result in the ultimate collapse of the entire architecture.
evidence: This is inferred from theoretical analysis of the architectures.

claim: Deducing regulatory architectures from outcomes after perturbations is complicated by multiple HRAs resulting in the same HRA when perturbed.
source: Deducing regulatory architectures from outcomes after perturbations is complicated by multiple HRAs resulting in the same HRA when perturbed (e.g. 16 HRAs can result in 'A' when perturbed, Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Of 225,000 ESP systems simulated, 78,285 had heritable regulatory architectures that remained after 250 generations.
source: Of 225,000 ESP systems thus simulated, 78,285 had heritable regulatory architectures that remained after 250 generations (system-ids and other details for exploration of individual systems are in Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct result from the simulations performed.

claim: An excess of positive regulatory links was needed to sustain a system with negative regulatory links.
source: Furthermore, an excess of positive regulatory links was needed to sustain a system with negative regulatory links (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, right), with the minimal system that can sustain a negative regulatory interaction requiring three sensors, as expected.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The minimal system that can sustain a negative regulatory interaction requires three sensors.
source: Furthermore, an excess of positive regulatory links was needed to sustain a system with negative regulatory links (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, right), with the minimal system that can sustain a negative regulatory interaction requiring three sensors, as expected.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations and is consistent with theoretical expectations.

claim: Of the 78,285 stable systems, 14,180 showed heritable epigenetic change.
source: Of the 78,285 stable systems, 14,180 showed heritable epigenetic change.
evidence: This is stated as a result from simulations shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The heritability of regulatory architectures that are intrinsically unstable can be enhanced through interactions that alter the regulation of one or more sensors.
source: Collectively, these results reveal that the heritability of regulatory architectures that are intrinsically unstable can be enhanced through interactions that alter the regulation of one or more sensors.
evidence: This is inferred from simulation results showing effects of periodic perturbations.

claim: External regulators that enhance heritability of unstable architectures could be part of the environment or other cells.
source: Such external regulators could be part of the environment (e.g. periodic interactions such as circadian signals) or other cells (e.g. periodic interactions with somatic cells for regulatory architectures transmitted along a germline).
evidence: This is a speculative inference about possible sources of external regulation.

claim: 14 cell divisions are necessary to go from the zygote of one generation to the zygote of the next in C. elegans.
source: For example, 14 cell divisions are necessary to go from the zygote of one generation to the zygote of the next (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on curated data from the literature about C. elegans development.

claim: Parental rde-4 can enable RNA silencing in adult rde-4(-) progeny.
source: For example, parental rde-4 can enable RNA silencing in adult rde-4(-) progeny (Marré et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Loss of meg-3/4 can result in persistent RNA silencing defects despite restoration of wild-type meg-3/4 for multiple generations.
source: Furthermore, loss of meg-3/–4 can result in persistent RNA silencing defects despite restoration of wild-type meg-3/–4 for multiple generations (Dodson and Kennedy, 2019; Lev et al., 2019; Ouyang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Of 10,000 ESP systems simulated with developmental timing and regulatory delays, 11 maintained all entities/sensors for 10 generations.
source: Of the 10,000 such ESP systems simulated, 11 maintained all entities/sensors for 10 generations (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a direct result from simulations incorporating C. elegans developmental timing.

claim: The transgenerational waveforms traced by the relative numbers of all entities/sensors reveal periods of increased expression/activity for some entities/sensors during development.
source: The transgenerational waveforms traced by the relative numbers of all entities/sensors reveal periods of increased expression/activity for some entities/sensors during development (red asterisks in Figure 5d), as observed for many genes expressed in the germline.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 5D and compared to known biological observations.

claim: 22G RNAs and pUG RNAs are experimentally measurable molecular markers whose levels are thought to be proportional to the extent of gene silencing.
source: 22G RNAs and pUG RNAs are experimentally measurable molecular markers whose levels are thought to be proportional to the extent of gene silencing (e.g. Gu et al., 2009; Pak et al., 2012; Shirayama et al., 2012), although formally gene-specific regulatory features could influence this proportionality (Knudsen et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work, with a caveat noted.

claim: The maintenance of RNA silencing across generations is thought to require a positive feedback loop formed by antisense small RNAs called 22G RNAs that are bound to the Argonaute HRDE-1 and sense mRNA fragments processed into poly-UG RNAs (pUG RNAs).
source: The maintenance of RNA silencing across generations is thought to require a positive feedback loop formed by antisense small RNAs called 22G RNAs that are bound to the Argonaute HRDE-1 (Buckley et al., 2012) and sense mRNA fragments processed into poly-UG RNAs (pUG RNAs) (Shukla et al., 2020) that can act as templates for RNA-dependent RNA polymerases that synthesize the 22G RNAs.
evidence: This is based on citations to prior experimental work.

claim: When a gene silenced by disrupting RNA regulation within the germline is exposed to genes with matching sequences, different outcomes are possible.
source: For example, when a gene silenced by disrupting RNA regulation within the germline (iT, a transgene with silenced mCherry sequences) is exposed to genes with matching sequences (Figure 6, Devanapally et al., 2021), different outcomes are possible.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from Devanapally et al., 2021.

claim: After initial silencing in trans, newly exposed genes can recover from silencing when separated from the source of silencing signals.
source: After initial silencing in trans, the newly exposed genes can recover from silencing (mCherry and mCherry∆pi in Figure 6a) when separated from the source of silencing signals
evidence: This is based on experimental data from Devanapally et al., 2021 shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Newly exposed genes can be either continually silenced or become resistant to silencing depending on the presence of intact piRNA-binding sequences despite the continued presence of the source.
source: but can be either continually silenced (mCherry/iT in Figure 6a) or become resistant to silencing (mCherry∆pi/iT in Figure 6a) depending on the presence of intact piRNA-binding sequences despite the continued presence of the source.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from Devanapally et al., 2021 shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Recognition of the target mRNA by piRNAs prolongs RNA silencing.
source: While this observation suggests that recognition of the target mRNA by piRNAs prolongs RNA silencing, loss of the Argonaute PRG-1 that binds piRNAs and regulates more than 3000 genes in the germline (e.g. Reed et al., 2020) also prolongs the duration of heritable RNA silencing (Shukla et al., 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations cited.

claim: Loss of the Argonaute PRG-1 that binds piRNAs and regulates more than 3000 genes in the germline also prolongs the duration of heritable RNA silencing.
source: While this observation suggests that recognition of the target mRNA by piRNAs prolongs RNA silencing, loss of the Argonaute PRG-1 that binds piRNAs and regulates more than 3000 genes in the germline (e.g. Reed et al., 2020) also prolongs the duration of heritable RNA silencing (Shukla et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from cited studies.

claim: A chromodomain protein HERI-1 has been reported to be recruited to genes undergoing heritable RNA silencing and is required to limit the duration of the silencing.
source: Consistently, a chromodomain protein HERI-1 has been reported to be recruited to genes undergoing heritable RNA silencing and is required to limit the duration of the silencing (Perales et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on experimental work cited.

claim: The dynamics of recovery from silencing depends on the strength of an inhibitory feedback that can act across generations to reduce the HRDE-1-dependent positive feedback loop.
source: Specifically, the dynamics of recovery from silencing depends on the strength of an inhibitory feedback that can act across generations to reduce the HRDE-1-dependent positive feedback loop.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism based on theoretical analysis and experimental data.

claim: The transgenerational inhibition relies on sensor(s) that are regulated by PRG-1 and is opposed by piRNA binding to the silenced mRNA.
source: This transgenerational inhibition relies on sensor(s) that are regulated by PRG-1 and is opposed by piRNA binding to the silenced mRNA (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The genome likely interacts with the largest number of sensors per molecule, making it the entity with the most information density.
source: The genome likely interacts with the largest number of sensors per molecule, making it the entity with the most information density.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about information density in biological systems.

claim: When a gene sequence is transcribed and translated, sequence information is transmitted from one molecule (DNA) to many (RNA(s) and/or protein(s)), thereby reducing the density of sequence information per entity.
source: When a gene sequence is transcribed and translated, sequence information is transmitted from one molecule (DNA) to many (RNA(s) and/or protein(s)), thereby reducing the density of sequence information per entity (e.g. RNA or protein of a particular sequence).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of molecular biology and information theory.

claim: Information is added to RNAs and proteins through the process of RNA folding and protein folding, which depend on interactions with the surrounding chemical and physical context.
source: However, information is also added to these entities through the process of RNA folding and protein folding, which depend on interactions with the surrounding chemical and physical context (e.g. Porter and Looger, 2018).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of molecular biology supported by a citation.

claim: Only a small number of possible regulatory architectures formed by a set of interactors are heritable.
source: Only a small number of possible regulatory architectures formed by a set of interactors are heritable.
evidence: This is stated as a principle derived from the analysis.

claim: Maintenance of heritable regulatory architectures for many generations requires positive feedback loops.
source: Their maintenance for many generations requires positive feedback loops.
evidence: This is stated as a principle derived from theoretical analysis.

claim: Heritable regulatory architectures carry a vast amount of information that can quickly outstrip the information that can be stored in genomes as the number of interactors increase.
source: Such heritable regulatory architectures carry a vast amount of information that can quickly outstrip the information that can be stored in genomes as the number of interactors increase.
evidence: This is inferred from the calculations shown in Table 1.

claim: Transient perturbations reveal diagnostic differences between regulatory architectures.
source: Transient perturbations reveal diagnostic differences between regulatory architectures and suggest ways to generate heritable epigenetic changes for particular architectures.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations in Figure 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: Transgenerational inhibition that tunes the activity of positive feedback loops in regulatory architectures can explain the gene-specific dynamics of heritable RNA silencing observed in C. elegans.
source: Transgenerational inhibition that tunes the activity of positive feedback loops in regulatory architectures can explain the gene-specific dynamics of heritable RNA silencing observed in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.
evidence: This is the proposed explanation based on theoretical modeling and experimental data.

claim: Only 7 of the 13 possible 3-node graphs formed by 3 interactors can be HRAs.
source: Imposing the need for positive regulation for heritability reveals that only 7 of the 13 possible 3-node graphs formed by 3 interactors can be HRAs
evidence: This is stated as a result of computational enumeration.

claim: Only 125 of the 199 possible 4-node graphs can be HRAs.
source: and only 125 of the 199 possible 4-node graphs can be HRAs (see Methods for computation).
evidence: This is stated as a result of computational enumeration.

claim: Perpetual inheritance of regulatory architectures requires sustained production of all the interacting molecules.
source: Perpetual inheritance of such regulatory architectures requires sustained production of all the interacting molecules, that is every interactor must have regulatory input that promotes its production to overcome dilution at every cell division and other turnover mechanisms, if any.
evidence: This is a fundamental requirement derived from theoretical considerations.

claim: Every interactor must have regulatory input that promotes its production to overcome dilution at every cell division and other turnover mechanisms.
source: Perpetual inheritance of such regulatory architectures requires sustained production of all the interacting molecules, that is every interactor must have regulatory input that promotes its production to overcome dilution at every cell division and other turnover mechanisms, if any.
evidence: This is a fundamental requirement derived from theoretical considerations.

claim: This requirement for sustained production was fundamental for conceiving the origin of life and remains necessary for its persistence.
source: Indeed, this requirement was fundamental for conceiving the origin of life (Eigen, 1971; Gánti, 1975; Varela et al., 1974; Kauffman, 1993) and remains necessary for its persistence.
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work on the origin of life.
